topic.title: Gradient at a point on a curve as instantaneous rate of change (tangents)
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: Almost every series on M8 Paper 2, as the closing 2 marks of a 6-8 mark graph question. Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9 (draw an exponential graph 3, read when it had trebled 1, rate from a tangent 2: only the better candidates drew the tangent); Summer 2023 Paper 2 Q11 (sketch a decay curve 4, a reading 2, the rate of decay 2: the tangent only by the best); November 2024 Paper 2 Q10 (draw an exponential curve, use it, interpret the multiplier: the reading part answered by fewer than half).
mustMemorise: Rate of change at a point = gradient of the tangent drawn there
Average rate over an interval = gradient of the chord joining its ends
Gradient = rise ÷ run, read from the axes and never counted in squares
Units of a rate = unit of the vertical axis ÷ unit of the horizontal axis

note.title: Gradient at a point: rate of change from a tangent
note.subject: maths

given: Nothing for this topic. The Higher sheet carries the prism, the trapezium, the sphere, the cone, the quadratic formula, the sine and cosine rules and ½ab sin C, and nothing else.
mustKnow: Rate of change at a point = gradient of the tangent drawn at that point
Average rate over an interval = gradient of the chord joining its two ends
Gradient = rise ÷ run, both read from the axes, never counted in squares
Units of a rate = unit of the vertical axis ÷ unit of the horizontal axis
A negative gradient means the quantity is falling; on a velocity-time graph that is deceleration

notOnThisSpec: Differentiation: the gradient is estimated from a drawn tangent, never calculated from a derivative
Area under a curve, and distance from a velocity-time graph
Rates of change of anything that is not shown as a graph

mustBeAbleTo: Draw a tangent to a curve at a stated point, with a ruler and long enough to read from
Find its gradient from two well-separated points, using the axis scales rather than counting squares
Give the answer with the units the axes imply, and with the right sign
Find an average rate of change as the gradient of a chord between two points on the curve
Explain the difference between an average rate and a rate at an instant, and say which is larger for a curve that steepens
Interpret the gradient of a distance-time graph as speed and of a velocity-time graph as acceleration
Read values and times from a growth or decay curve to the accuracy the grid allows
Say what a gradient means in the words of the context: cooling so many degrees each minute, slowing by so many metres per second each second
Find where on a curve the rate equals an average, by a tangent parallel to the chord (going further)
Say where a curve's rate is zero: where its tangent is flat
sheet.howExamined: M8 Paper 2 (calculator, 75 minutes, 50 marks) carries this most series, as the closing marks of a graph question worth 6 to 8: draw the curve from a formula (3), read a value or a time from it (1), then 'by drawing a suitable line, estimate the rate' (2). Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9 ran exactly that way, and Summer 2023 Paper 2 Q11 the same with a decay curve; a pure curve's gradient has also been asked (Summer 2019 Paper 2 Q13, Summer 2021 Paper 1 Q13). Schemes give MA1 for the tangent drawn at the stated point and MA1 for a value from the drawn tangent, within a generous band.
traps: Not drawing a tangent at all: only the better candidates drew one, and not all of those could work out its gradient (Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9)
Leaving the rate of decay unanswered: the tangent was completed only by the best candidates (Summer 2023 Paper 2 Q11)
An awkward grid scale makes a smooth curve hard to draw: plot each point with care and join them with one smooth curve (Summer 2023 Paper 2 Q11)
Losing the mark for the value at t = 0 on an exponential curve: the multiplier to the power 0 is 1 (Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9)
Misusing your own curve: fewer than half answered the part that used the curve they had drawn (November 2024 Paper 2 Q10)
Using a chord between two points on the curve, which gives an average rather than an instantaneous rate
Counting squares for rise and run without converting to the units on the axes
Taking two points close together, so a small reading slip changes the gradient badly
Dropping the minus sign on a falling curve, which turns cooling into warming and braking into speeding up
Giving a rate without the units the axes imply
Computing the rate from the formula when the part says to use the graph

noteBlocks.lede: A straight line has one gradient everywhere; a curve's gradient changes from point to point. The gradient of the tangent at a point, the straight line that runs along the curve there, is how fast the quantity is changing at that moment: its instantaneous rate of change.
can: Draw a tangent at a stated point and find its gradient from two far-apart points on it.
Tell an average rate over an interval (a chord) from a rate at one instant (a tangent).
Give a rate with its units and its sign, and say what it means in the story.

noteBlocks.caption: The curve gets steeper, so her speed keeps changing; the tangent at P runs along the curve there.

noteBlocks.md: A cyclist's distance-time graph curves upwards: she is speeding up, so her speed is different at every moment. Her speed at one instant is the gradient of the tangent there, the straight line that touches the curve at that point and runs along it. Read two points on the tangent and work out rise over run. On a straight line you read the gradient once; on a curve you choose the moment first.

noteBlocks.stem: The tangent to the cyclist's graph at $P$, where $t = 4$, passes through $(2, 0)$ and $(8, 24)$. Estimate her speed at $t = 4$ s.

steps.decision: Read both points from the axes; the vertical axis is in metres.
The horizontal axis is in seconds.

steps.working: Gradient $= 24 \div 6 = 4$, so her speed at $t = 4$ is about $4$ m/s
steps.decision: Metres over seconds: the units come off the axes.

noteBlocks.prompt: A tangent to a distance-time graph, in metres and seconds, passes through $(1, 2)$ and $(5, 20)$. What speed does it give?
noteBlocks.explain: Rise $= 20 - 2 = 18$ m and run $= 5 - 1 = 4$ s, so the gradient is $18 \div 4 = 4.5$ m/s.

twin.prompt: A tangent to a distance-time graph, in metres and seconds, passes through $(2, 3)$ and $(7, 33)$. What speed does it give?
twin.explain: Rise $= 33 - 3 = 30$ m, run $= 7 - 2 = 5$ s, so the gradient is $30 \div 5 = 6$ m/s.

optionNotes.why: 33 is a distance read off the line, not a rate.
$33 \div 7$ joins the origin to a point: a chord, so an average.
Run over rise turns the gradient upside down.
20 is how far she has gone at that point, a value on the tangent, not how fast the distance is changing.
$20 \div 5$ is the gradient of a chord from the origin, an average since the start.
That is run over rise; a gradient is rise over run.

noteBlocks.text: Why the tangent gives the instant rate

noteBlocks.md: An average speed over an interval is the gradient of a chord: change in distance over change in time. Shrink the interval towards one moment and the chord swings round until it lies along the tangent. So the tangent's gradient is where those averages end up: the speed at that instant. You never need the chords in an exam, but they are why the method works.

noteBlocks.caption: As the second point closes in on P, the chord turns towards the tangent.

noteBlocks.stem: On the cyclist's graph, chords from $P$ at $t = 4$ run to $t = 8$, $t = 6$ and $t = 5$. What do their gradients approach?

steps.decision: The average speed over four seconds.
A shorter interval, a smaller average: she was slower at the start of it.
Shorter again.

steps.working: The averages close in on $4$ m/s, the gradient of the tangent at $P$
steps.decision: Each shorter interval is a better average for the one moment; the tangent is where they end up.

noteBlocks.prompt: Chords from the point where $t = 3$ on a curve have gradients $9$, $7.5$, $6.6$ and $6.3$ as the other end closes in. What is the gradient of the tangent at $t = 3$?
noteBlocks.explain: The chords' gradients fall towards 6 as the interval shrinks, so the tangent, where they end up, has gradient about 6.

twin.prompt: Chords from the point where $t = 1$ on a curve have gradients $2.2$, $1.6$, $1.3$ and $1.1$ as the other end closes in. What is the gradient of the tangent at $t = 1$?
twin.explain: The gradients fall towards 1 as the chord shrinks, so the tangent at $t = 1$ has gradient about 1.

optionNotes.why: 2.2 belongs to the longest chord, the furthest from the tangent.
The mean of the four is not their limit; they fall towards 1.
The chords are not flattening to 0; they settle near 1.
9 is the gradient of the longest chord, the roughest average of all.
Averaging the chords' gradients does not find where they are heading; they head for 6.
The chords all slope upwards, so the tangent is not flat.

noteBlocks.text: Chord or tangent: read the question

noteBlocks.md: Two questions, two lines. *Over* an interval asks for an average: draw the chord joining its two ends. *At* or *when* asks for one instant: draw the tangent there. On a curve that bends, the two answers differ, so the wording decides which line you draw. Underline the words that name the time before you pick up the ruler.

noteBlocks.text: The units come off the axes

noteBlocks.md: A gradient is a rate, and its unit is the vertical axis's unit over the horizontal axis's. Metres against seconds give m/s, a speed; velocity in m/s against seconds gives m/s², an acceleration; litres against minutes give litres per minute. Read the axis labels before you write the answer. In an interpretation part the units are often worth a mark of their own.

noteBlocks.title: Why the units divide
noteBlocks.md: A gradient divides a change in the vertical quantity by a change in the horizontal one, so its units divide in the same way: metres by seconds, litres by minutes.

steps.decision: Metres over seconds: a speed.

steps.working: Velocity (m/s) against time (s): m/s²
steps.decision: Metres per second, per second: an acceleration.

steps.working: Volume (litres) against time (minutes): litres per minute
steps.decision: Always the vertical unit over the horizontal one.

noteBlocks.text: The sign says rising or falling

noteBlocks.md: A tangent sloping down has a negative gradient, and the minus sign is part of the answer: it says the quantity is falling. On a velocity graph a negative gradient is a deceleration: the vehicle is slowing down.

A seedling grows. The graph shows its height $H$ cm after $t$ weeks.

(a) Estimate the average rate of growth over the first 6 weeks.
(b) Estimate the rate of growth at the instant $t = 6$ weeks.
(c) Explain why the two answers differ.

figure.alt: A graph of a seedling's height in cm up to 30 against time in weeks up to 9. The curve starts just above the time axis and bends upwards. A dotted chord joins the start to the point at t = 6, and a dashed tangent touches the curve at t = 6.

steps.working: Average rate $= \dfrac{14 - 2}{6 - 0} = 2$ cm per week
steps.decision: An average over an interval is the gradient of the chord: change in height over change in time.

steps.working: Draw the tangent at $t = 6$ with a ruler
steps.decision: The rate at one instant needs the tangent, because the growth is speeding up all the way along.

options.text: A tangent touching the curve at $t = 6$
options.feedback: The rate at one instant is the gradient of the tangent there.
A chord gives an average over an interval.
A vertical line has no gradient to read.

steps.working: Two points on the tangent: $(3, 2)$ and $(9, 26)$. Gradient $= \dfrac{26 - 2}{9 - 3} = 4$
steps.decision: Points six weeks apart, so a small misreading barely moves the result.

steps.working: About $4$ cm per week
steps.decision: Centimetres over weeks.

options.feedback: The vertical unit over the horizontal unit.
That turns the rate upside down.
A height alone is not a rate.

steps.working: $4 > 2$, because the curve gets steeper
steps.decision: The average includes the slow early weeks; the rate at the end is measured where the curve is steepest.

accepted: The curve gets steeper, so the rate at the end is bigger than the average

items.skill: Choose the right line for a rate at an instant

options.text: A tangent touching the curve at $t = 4$
options.feedback: The tangent matches the curve's direction at that one point, so its gradient is the rate at that instant.
A chord measures the average rate across the whole interval, not the rate at the end of it.
A vertical line has no gradient at all. The rate is a slope, so the line has to lie along the curve.

options.text: Nothing: read the value of the curve at $t = 4$
options.feedback: That gives the quantity itself, not how fast it is changing. Summer 2024 examiners reported that only the stronger candidates thought to draw a tangent.

items.stem: A graph has temperature in °C up the side and time in minutes along the bottom. What are the units of its gradient?

options.feedback: Units of the vertical axis divided by units of the horizontal axis, every time.
That is the unit of the temperature itself. A gradient is a change in temperature divided by a change in time, so it carries both units.
That is the gradient upside down. Rise over run means the vertical unit comes first.
A rate always has units, and an interpretation part gives a mark for them.

items.stem: On a distance-time curve, the chord across the whole journey has gradient $2.5$ and the tangent at $t = 6$ s has gradient $3$. What is the speed at $t = 6$ s?

options.feedback: The tangent touches at that instant, so its gradient is the speed then.
That is the average speed over the whole journey. It answers a different question.
Adding the two rates together has no meaning. Each line answers its own question.
$9$ is the distance travelled by then, read from the vertical axis, not a speed.

items.stem: One small square is 0.2 seconds across and 1 metre up. A tangent rises 4 squares over a run of 5 squares. What is its gradient?
items.skill: Read a gradient with the axis scales

options.feedback: Rise $= 4$ m, run $= 1$ s, so the gradient is $4 \div 1 = 4$ m/s.
That divides squares by squares. The two axes have different scales, so turn the squares into metres and seconds first.
That is run ÷ rise. Gradient is rise ÷ run.
The two scales have been applied to the wrong axes: the 0.2 belongs to the horizontal run, and the 1 metre to the vertical rise.

items.stem: A cooling curve falls as time goes on. What can you say about the gradient of a tangent drawn on it?
items.skill: Read the sign of a rate

options.text: It is negative, because the temperature is falling as time increases
options.feedback: A falling curve has a negative gradient, and the minus sign is the part of the answer that says 'cooling'.

options.text: It is positive, because temperature and time are both positive
options.feedback: The sign of the gradient comes from the direction of the line, not from the values on the axes.

options.text: It is zero, because the curve levels off
options.feedback: The curve flattens as it goes, but at any point before that it still has a definite negative slope.

options.text: It has no sign: a rate is always positive
options.feedback: A rate of change is signed. Negative means falling, positive means rising, and an examiner reads the sign as information.

items.stem: You have drawn a tangent. Which two points should you use to find its gradient?
items.skill: Pick two points on the tangent

options.text: Two points on the tangent, as far apart as the grid allows
options.feedback: Far-apart points on the drawn line make a small reading error much less damaging.

options.text: Two points on the curve either side of the contact point
options.feedback: Those two points define a chord, which gives an average rate rather than the rate at the instant.

options.text: The contact point and one other point on the curve
options.feedback: One of the points is off the tangent, so what you measure is a chord again.

options.text: Two points on the tangent very close together
options.feedback: Close points are on the right line but make the reading unreliable: a half-square slip changes the gradient a great deal.

items.stem: A velocity-time graph has gradient $-3$ at $t = 5$ s. What does that mean?

options.text: The tram is slowing by about $3$ m/s every second
options.feedback: The number is the size of the change each second; the minus sign says the velocity is falling.

options.text: The tram is travelling at $3$ m/s
options.feedback: The velocity is read from the vertical axis. The gradient tells you how fast that velocity is changing.

options.text: The tram travels $3$ m in the next second
options.feedback: A velocity-time gradient is about change in speed, not distance covered.

options.text: The tram is speeding up by $3$ m/s each second
options.feedback: The gradient is negative, so the velocity is going down, not up.

items.stem: A duckweed graph is at $A = 20.25$ m² when $t = 4$ weeks. A part asks for the rate of increase at that moment. Which answer is right?
items.skill: Know what a rate is not

options.text: About $8.2$ m² per week, from the gradient of a tangent at $t = 4$
options.feedback: A rate is a gradient, and at a single instant it is the gradient of the tangent there.
That is how much duckweed there is, not how fast the amount is changing.
Dividing the area by the time gives an average across the whole four weeks, which is not the rate at the end of them.
The number is right, and a rate needs its units: square metres per week. An interpretation part gives a separate mark for them.

items.stem: A tangent to a graph of volume in litres against time in minutes passes through $(0, 4)$ and $(5, 24)$. What rate does it give?
items.skill: Read a rate from two points on a drawn tangent, with its units

options.feedback: Rise $= 20$ litres over a run of 5 minutes: 4 litres per minute.
24 is a volume read off the line, not a rate.
$24 \div 5$ joins the origin to a point on the line: rise is $24 - 4 = 20$, not 24.
That is run over rise, upside down.

figures.alt: A cooling curve: temperature in degrees Celsius falling from 80 at t = 0 and levelling off towards 20, with time in minutes on the horizontal axis up to 10.

parts.stem:
Use the graph to **estimate** how long the tea takes to cool to 40 °C.

Answer ________ minutes

scheme.for: 3.8 read from the graph

hints: Find 40 on the temperature axis.
Go across to the curve, then straight down.
Each small square across is 0.2 minutes.
parts.workedSolution: Going across from $T = 40$ to the curve and down to the time axis gives about $3.8$ minutes. The exact value is $3.819\ldots$, so any reading from 3.62 to 4.02 is accepted.

context.setting: A duckweed growth curve

figures.alt: The same growth curve with a dashed straight tangent drawn touching it at t = 4 weeks.

parts.stem:
The tangent to the duckweed curve at $t = 4$ weeks has been drawn.

**Estimate** the rate at which the area is increasing at that moment.

Answer ________ m² per week

scheme.for: tangent drawn at the stated point, and rise ÷ run attempted from two points on it
about 8.2

hints: Draw the tangent with a ruler so it touches at that point.
Choose two points on the tangent that are far apart.
Rise ÷ run, reading both from the axes rather than counting squares.
parts.workedSolution: Two points on the tangent are $(2, 3.8)$ and $(6, 36.7)$. Gradient $= \dfrac{36.7 - 3.8}{6 - 2} = 8.2$ m² per week.

commonErrors.feedback: $20.25$ m² is the area at that moment, read off the vertical axis. The rate is how fast the area is changing, which is the gradient of the tangent: about $8.2$ m² per week.

questions.solutionProgram: tangent at t = 4 on A = 4(1.5)^t; gradient 4*1.5^4*ln1.5

context.setting: Average against instantaneous rate on a growth curve

figures.alt: The same growth curve with a dashed straight tangent drawn touching it at t = 4 weeks.

parts.stem:
Work out the average rate at which the duckweed area grew over the first 4 weeks.

Answer ________ m² per week
hints: An average rate is a change divided by the time it took.
Read the area at $t = 0$ and at $t = 4$ from the graph.
parts.workedSolution: The area grows from $4$ m² to $20.25$ m² in 4 weeks, so the average rate is $\dfrac{20.25 - 4}{4} = 4.06$ m² per week.

commonErrors.feedback: $8.2$ m² per week is the rate at the single instant $t = 4$, from the tangent. An average across the four weeks is the chord: $\dfrac{20.25 - 4}{4} = 4.06$.

parts.stem:
The rate at the instant $t = 4$ weeks is about $8.2$ m² per week.

Explain why this is larger than your answer to part (a).

accepted: The growth is speeding up, so the rate at the end of the interval is greater than the average across it

scheme.for: the curve gets steeper, so the rate at the end of the four weeks is greater than the average over them

hints: Compare the steepness of the curve at the start and at the end.
parts.workedSolution: The curve gets steeper as time goes on. The average of $4.06$ m² per week is spread across four weeks that include the slow start, while $8.2$ m² per week is measured at the end, where the curve is steepest.

questions.solutionProgram: average over 0..4 = (A(4)-A(0))/4; instantaneous at 4 from the tangent

context.setting: Reading a gradient when one small square is not one unit

figures.alt: The same distance-time curve with a dashed straight tangent drawn touching it at t = 6 seconds, where the distance is 9 metres.

parts.stem:
On this grid one small square is 0.2 seconds across and 1 metre up.

A student draws a tangent that rises 5 small squares over a run of 4 small squares.

Work out the gradient this tangent represents.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: rise = 5 m and run = 0.8 s (the scales used)

hints: Turn the squares into metres and seconds first.
5 squares up is 5 m; 4 squares across is 0.8 s.
Then divide.
parts.workedSolution: The rise is $5 \times 1 = 5$ m and the run is $4 \times 0.2 = 0.8$ s. Gradient $= 5 \div 0.8 = 6.25$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides squares by squares. The axes are not both one unit per square here: the run of 4 squares is only $0.8$ seconds, which makes the gradient $6.25$ m/s.

questions.solutionProgram: one small square is 0.2 s by 1 m; a tangent rising 5 squares over 4 squares

context.setting: Reading a time from a growth curve

figures.alt: A growth curve: the area of duckweed in square metres rising from 4 at t = 0 to about 45 at t = 6, with time in weeks on the horizontal axis.

parts.stem:
Use the graph to **estimate** when the duckweed first covered 20 m².

Answer ________ weeks

scheme.for: 4 read from the graph

hints: Find 20 on the area axis.
Go across to the curve and down to the time axis.
parts.workedSolution: Reading across from $A = 20$ to the curve and down gives about $4$ weeks; the exact value is $3.969\ldots$ weeks.

parts.stem:
Two dashed straight lines are drawn on this graph: a chord from end to end, and a tangent at $t = 6$ s.

Describe what the gradient of each one measures.

accepted: The chord gives the average speed over the whole journey; the tangent gives the speed at the instant t = 6 s

scheme.for: chord = average rate over the interval
tangent = rate at that single instant

hints: One line touches the curve at a single point; the other joins two points on it.
Which of those could describe a whole journey?
parts.workedSolution: The chord joins the start and the end, so its gradient is the total distance divided by the total time: the average speed, $2.5$ m/s. The tangent touches at one point only, so its gradient is the speed at that instant, about $3$ m/s.

A mug of tea is left in a room. Its temperature $T$ °C after $t$ minutes is given by $T = 20 + 60(0.75)^t$.

a smooth curve through the points, falling steeply then levelling off towards 20 °C

The curve flattens but never drops below the room temperature of 20 °C.
parts.workedSolution: The table is (0, 80), (1, 65), (2, 53.8), (3, 45.3), (4, 39), (5, 34.2), (6, 30.7), (7, 28), (8, 26), (9, 24.5), (10, 23.4). Plot all eleven points and join them with one smooth curve: steep at first, flattening towards 20 °C without ever reaching it.

parts.stem:
By drawing a suitable line, **estimate** the rate at which the tea is cooling when $t = 4$ minutes.

parts.stem:
Duckweed spreads across a pond. Its area $A$ m² after $t$ weeks is given by $A = 4(1.5)^t$.

Draw the graph of $A$ against $t$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ on the grid.

scheme.for: all seven points plotted correctly, including the starting value at t = 0
a smooth curve through the points, rising more and more steeply

hints: Work out each value before plotting anything.
The curve gets steeper as it goes.
parts.workedSolution: The table is (0, 4), (1, 6), (2, 9), (3, 13.5), (4, 20.25), (5, 30.38), (6, 45.56). Plot all seven points and join them with one smooth curve that steepens as it rises.

parts.stem:
Use your graph to **estimate** when the area had trebled from its starting value.

Answer ________ weeks

Three times that is $12$ m².
Read across from that value to the curve and down.
parts.workedSolution: Three times the starting area is $12$ m². Reading across from $12$ to the curve and down to the time axis gives about $2.7$ weeks.

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is the multiplier, not the time. Treble the starting area to get $12$ m², then read across to the curve: the answer is about $2.7$ weeks.

Rise ÷ run, reading both from the axes rather than counting squares.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the distance a sledge has travelled against time.

Work out the sledge's average speed over the 10 seconds shown.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: 25 ÷ 10 seen, or the chord used

hints: Total distance ÷ total time.
Read the distance at $t = 10$ s.
parts.workedSolution: The sledge covers $25$ m in $10$ s, so its average speed is $25 \div 10 = 2.5$ m/s. That is the gradient of the chord.

parts.stem:
**Estimate** the sledge's speed at the instant $t = 6$ s.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: tangent drawn at the stated point, and rise ÷ run attempted from two points on it
about 3

hints: Draw the tangent with a ruler so it touches at that point.
Choose two points on the tangent that are far apart.
Rise ÷ run, reading both from the axes rather than counting squares.
parts.workedSolution: The tangent at $t = 6$ passes through $(3, 0)$ and $(9, 18)$, so the gradient is $\dfrac{18}{6} = 3$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: $2.5$ m/s is the average over the whole journey, from the chord. For the speed at one instant the line has to touch the curve at that point: the tangent gives about $3$ m/s.
$9$ m is the distance travelled by $t = 6$ s, read from the vertical axis. The speed is the gradient there, about $3$ m/s.

parts.stem: Explain why your two answers are different.

accepted: The sledge is speeding up, so its speed at t = 6 s is greater than its average over the whole journey

scheme.for: the sledge is speeding up: the curve gets steeper, so the speed at t = 6 s exceeds the average over the whole 10 s

hints: Compare the steepness of the curve at the beginning and at the end.
parts.workedSolution: The curve gets steeper as time goes on, so the sledge is speeding up. The average of $2.5$ m/s includes the slow start, while $3$ m/s is measured at one later instant.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the velocity of a tram as it brakes. A tangent has been drawn at $t = 5$ s.

**Estimate** the tram's acceleration at that instant.

Answer ________ m/s²

scheme.for: tangent drawn touching the curve at the stated point
two points on the tangent read from the axes and rise ÷ run formed
about -3

hints: Draw the tangent with a ruler so it touches at that point.
Choose two points on the tangent that are far apart.
Rise ÷ run, reading both from the axes rather than counting squares.
parts.workedSolution: Two points on the tangent are $(2, 31.5)$ and $(8, 13.5)$. Gradient $= \dfrac{13.5 - 31.5}{8 - 2} = -3$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right. The tangent slopes downwards, so the gradient is negative: $-3$ m/s². Dropping the sign turns braking into speeding up.

parts.stem: Explain what your answer tells you about the tram, and why the gradient at $t = 0$ is different.

accepted: It is slowing by about 3 m/s each second at t = 5 s; at t = 0 the curve is momentarily flat, so the tram is not yet losing speed

scheme.for: the tram is slowing down by about 3 m/s each second
at t = 0 the curve is momentarily flat, so the gradient there is 0

hints: What does a negative gradient mean here?
Look at the direction of the curve at the very start.
parts.workedSolution: A gradient of $-3$ m/s² means the velocity drops by about $3$ m/s every second, so the tram is braking. At $t = 0$ the curve leaves the axis horizontally, so its gradient is $0$: the braking has not begun to bite, and the deceleration grows as time goes on.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the number of bacteria, $N$ thousand, after $t$ hours. A tangent has been drawn at $t = 3$.

On this grid one small square is $0.5$ hours across and $2$ thousand up.

**Estimate** the rate at which the number of bacteria is growing at $t = 3$. Give the units of your answer.

scheme.for: two points on the tangent read in axis units and rise / run formed, e.g. (2, 11) and (5, 47)
about 12 thousand per hour (accept 10.8 to 13.2)

hints: Read two points on the tangent from the axes, not by counting squares.
Rise in thousands over run in hours.
The tangent passes through $(2, 11)$ and $(5, 47)$.
parts.workedSolution: Two points on the tangent are $(2, 11)$ and $(5, 47)$. The rise is $47 - 11 = 36$ thousand and the run is $5 - 2 = 3$ hours, so the gradient is $36 \div 3 = 12$: the number is growing by about 12 thousand bacteria per hour at $t = 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: That counts squares: 18 squares up over 6 across. Each square is 2 thousand up and 0.5 hours across, so the rate is 36 thousand over 3 hours, 12 thousand per hour.
23 thousand is the number at $t = 3$, not how fast it is changing.
$(23 - 5) \div 3$ is the average rate since the start, a chord; the rate at $t = 3$ is the tangent's gradient.

questions.solutionProgram: N = 2t^2 + 5; tangent at t = 3: N = 12t - 13 through (2, 11) and (5, 47); gradient 12 thousand per hour; counting squares gives 3

The graph shows the area, $A$ km², of an oil spill $t$ hours after a leak. Over the first 6 hours the average rate of spreading is $3$ km² per hour.

a tangent drawn parallel to that chord, or tangents tried until one has gradient 3
about 3 hours (accept 2.6 to 3.4)

You want the point where the tangent has that same gradient.
Slide a ruler parallel to the chord until it just touches the curve.
parts.workedSolution: The chord from $(0, 1)$ to $(6, 19)$ has gradient $18 \div 6 = 3$. A tangent parallel to it touches the curve where $t = 3$: there the tangent through $(3, 5.5)$ also passes through $(5, 11.5)$, a gradient of $6 \div 2 = 3$. So the rate equals the average at about $t = 3$ hours.

parts.stem:
A laptop costs £800. Its value after $t$ years is £$V$, where $V = 800(0.85)^{t}$.

Work out $V$ when $t = 2$.
hints: Multiply by 800.

parts.stem: Draw the graph of $V = 800(0.85)^{t}$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ on the grid.

scheme.for: the seven points plotted correctly, the first at (0, 800)
a smooth curve through the points, falling and flattening

hints: Build the table first.
At $t = 0$ the value is 800: the multiplier to the power 0 is 1.
Join the points with one smooth curve, not straight segments.
parts.workedSolution: The table is (0, 800), (1, 680), (2, 578), (3, 491), (4, 418), (5, 355), (6, 302). Plot the seven points and join them with one smooth curve that falls and flattens.

commonErrors.feedback: The points are right, but a curve is drawn smooth, not with a ruler between the points.

parts.stem: Use your graph to **estimate** when the value falls to £400.

scheme.for: about 4.3 years, read from the candidate's curve

hints: Go across from £400 to the curve, then down to the time axis.
parts.workedSolution: Across from £400 to the curve and down gives about $4.3$ years (the exact value is $4.27$ to 2 decimal places).

parts.stem: By drawing a suitable line, **estimate** the rate at which the value is changing when $t = 3$. Give the units of your answer.

scheme.for: tangent drawn at t = 3 and rise / run formed from two points on it
about -80 pounds per year (accept -88 to -72)

hints: Draw the tangent at $t = 3$, where the value is about £491.
Read two far-apart points on it.
Pounds over years.
parts.workedSolution: The tangent at $t = 3$, where $V \approx 491$, passes through about $(1, 651)$ and $(5, 332)$, so the gradient is $\dfrac{332 - 651}{4} \approx -80$: the value is changing at about $-80$ pounds per year.

commonErrors.feedback: £491 is the value at $t = 3$; the rate is the gradient of the tangent there.
The size is right, but the curve falls, so the rate of change is negative.

parts.stem: What does the sign of your answer to part (d) tell you?

accepted: The value is falling: the laptop loses about £80 a year at that time

scheme.for: the value is decreasing (at that moment)

hints: A negative gradient means the vertical quantity is going down as time goes on.
parts.workedSolution: The minus sign means the value is falling: at $t = 3$ the laptop is losing value at about £80 a year.

findTheMistake.stem: Seán was asked to estimate the rate at which a mug of tea was cooling when $t = 4$ minutes. His working:
studentWorking: At t = 4 the temperature is about 39 °C
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 finds the gradient of the chord from $t = 0$ to $t = 4$, which is the average rate of cooling across those four minutes. The question asked for the rate at the single instant $t = 4$, and by then the tea is cooling much more slowly than it was at the start.
correction: Draw a tangent touching the curve at t = 4
Take two points on the tangent, for example (1, 55.4) and (7, 22.6)
findTheMistake.feedback: The two readings are accurate, which is worth having, and the arithmetic is right for the question it answers. The word 'when' is what changes everything: a rate at a stated moment needs a tangent. The Summer 2023 examiners reported that this tangent step was completed only by the best candidates.

findTheMistake.stem: Méabh drew a correct tangent on a distance-time graph and then found its gradient. One small square is 0.2 seconds across and 1 metre up. Her working:
studentWorking: It rises 18 small squares and runs across 30 small squares
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 divides squares by squares. The two axes are not on the same scale: 18 squares up is $18$ m, but 30 squares across is only $6$ s. Ignoring that makes the answer five times too small, and $0.6$ m/s for a sledge already several seconds into a slope should have looked wrong.
findTheMistake.feedback: Drawing the tangent is the step most candidates never reach, and it carries the method mark, so the hard part is already done. Convert squares into the units on the axes before dividing, and check the answer against the context: a sledge on a slope is not moving at half a metre per second by then.

findTheMistake.stem: Asked what the gradient of a velocity-time graph tells you at $t = 5$ s, Ruairí wrote:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 drops the minus sign. The tangent slopes downwards, so the gradient is $-3$, not $3$. That sign is the difference between a tram that is braking and one that is speeding up, and line 3 then describes the wrong motion. The units are missing as well.
correction: The velocity is falling by about 3 m/s every second
So the tram is slowing down, not accelerating
findTheMistake.feedback: The tangent and the size of the gradient are both right, and they earn the method mark. Read the direction of the line before you write the number, and finish with the units: the November 2024 examiners reported that the part asking what a gradient means was answered by only just over half the entry.

prompts.prompt: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph measure, and in what units?
prompts.answer: Acceleration, in m/s per second, written m/s².

prompts.prompt: The tangent slopes downwards. What must the answer include?
prompts.answer: The minus sign. A negative gradient means the quantity is falling: cooling, decaying, slowing down. Dropping it describes the opposite behaviour.

prompts.prompt: A tangent passes through (3, 0) and (9, 18) on a distance-time graph in metres and seconds. What is the speed there?
How do you estimate the rate of change at one point of a curve?
prompts.answer: Draw the tangent there, then find its gradient: rise over run.

prompts.prompt: Which line gives the rate at one instant?
prompts.answer: A tangent at that point; a chord gives only an average.

prompts.prompt: Where do the units of a gradient come from?
prompts.answer: The vertical axis's unit over the horizontal axis's unit, such as m/s.

prompts.prompt: Counting squares: what must you do before dividing rise by run?
prompts.answer: Convert squares into axis units, since the two scales differ.

prompts.prompt: On a steepening curve, which is bigger: the average rate or the end rate?
prompts.answer: The rate at the end, because the curve is steepest there.

findings.asked: Sketch a decay curve over four years, read a value from it, then find the rate of decay at a stated time.
findings.wentWrong: The chosen scale made a smooth curve hard to draw and markers were generous; the curve and the reading both scored acceptably. The tangent for the rate of decay was completed only by the best candidates.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the tangent with a ruler at the stated time and took two well-separated points off the axes to find its gradient.
findings.rule: A rate of change at a stated moment is the gradient of the tangent drawn there.

findings.asked: Draw an exponential growth graph, read when the starting value had trebled, then estimate the instantaneous rate of increase at a stated value of x.
findings.wentWrong: The majority drew the graph, with the value at x = 0 the common loss, and a majority read it correctly. Only the stronger candidates thought to draw a tangent, and not all of those could find its gradient.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Plotted the starting value correctly, then drew a long tangent and used two distant points on it with the axis scales.
findings.rule: Draw the tangent with a ruler, pick two far-apart points on it, and use the scales.

findings.asked: Draw a curve, use it, and interpret what a gradient means.
findings.wentWrong: The curves were generally good. The part that used the curve was answered by fewer than half, and the final part, choosing which percentage growth the graph showed, by just over half.
findings.rule: Say what the gradient measures, in the units of the axes, and in the language of the context.

insight.ruleToRemember: The gradient at a point on a curve is the gradient of the tangent drawn there; draw it with a ruler, use two distant points and the axis scales, and interpret it with units and a sign.
insight.aStarSignal: Drawing a tangent unprompted and turning its gradient into a rate with units and a direction.
